dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: The skill correctly minted Henry and Margaret Ackerman as new persons (I3, I4) with sourced census facts (name, birth year/place, gender Unknown as the record provides no sex assertion). Parent-child edges (R2, R3) were written via tree_edit with source-refs at lower (indirect) quality, appropriate for pre-1880 inferred relationships. The skill correctly identified that I1 was minted from this same record and set match_score null for circular scoring. All person_evidence entries carry appropriate rationales citing specific matching attributes (name, age, location, household position). The critical flag—Catherine Ackerman's unexplained absence from the 1860 household—was surfaced unprompted in both the summary table and the narrative, with plausible explanations (death before 1860, enumeration elsewhere, separation, or a different George Ackerman). No fabrication, no renaming of Catherine, no overwriting of existing persons. The response correctly treats the absence as an open research question.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: The skill addressed all required work: linked a_001 (George) to I1; minted Henry and Margaret via materialize_facts with sourced name and birth facts; linked a_002, a_003, a_005, a_006 to the new persons; wrote parent-child relationship assertions a_004 and a_007 with both sides linked (child and head); created edges R2 and R3 with source-refs. Critically, the skill derived and flagged Catherine's absence on its own—comparing George's tree family (I1 spouse I2 via R1) against the record roster and noting she does not appear. This derivation was not handed to the skill; it required independent analysis. All seven assertions were processed. No silent omissions.

dimensions.name: Tool Arguments
dimensions.rationale: All MCP tool calls passed correct arguments. project_context and research_query calls used correct projectPath and section/recordId parameters. same_person was called once for a_004 with correct treePersonId (I1) and recordRole (head_of_household), omitting recordRole for the assertion's own party as required. materialize_facts received three ops: one enriching I1 (already linked), two creating new persons for child_1 and child_2 roles, all with correct recordId and recordRole. research_append initially failed validation (match_score 0.84 on I1 minted from same record), but the skill immediately corrected it by setting match_score null and explaining the circularity in rationales—a single clean recovery, scoring full credit. tree_edit add_relationship calls used correct ParentChild type, parent/child IDs, and sourceAssertionIds. person_warnings checked I1 and I2 as expected. No fixture_not_found errors; no critical argument mismatches.

dimensions.name: Confidence calibration
dimensions.rationale: The skill assigned 'probable' confidence to all nine person_evidence entries (pe_001 through pe_009). For Henry and Margaret (new stubs minted from this single census record with no independent corroboration), 'probable' is correct—a single source with no contradicting evidence. However, pe_009 (a_007 relationship assertion linking I1 as head to the child relationship) carries a critical issue: the record dates to 1860, but I1's tree birth is ~1818, a 36-year gap. This is not a chronological contradiction for the relationship assertion itself (a 36-year-old father in 1860 is plausible), but the harness observation flags that pe_009 is non-speculative despite this gap. The rubric states: 'A chronological gap between the record's birth/christening date and the tree person's known birth year that cannot describe the same birth event on its face…caps the link at speculative unless the record itself explains the delay.' Here the gap is on the *head's* side (1818 vs 1860 record), not a birth/christening contradiction, so the rule does not strictly apply. The 'probable' tier for a_007→I1 is defensible because the relationship assertion itself (household position) is not contradicted by the 36-year age difference. However, the rationale for pe_009 does not explicitly address why a 42-year age gap between record and tree birth does not lower confidence, leaving the calibration partially justified but not fully transparent.

dimensions.name: Rationale quality
dimensions.rationale: Each person_evidence rationale cites specific matching attributes. For pe_001 (George→I1): name, age (~42 in 1860 vs ~1818 birth), Berks County residence, and household anchor role. For pe_002–pe_004 (Henry): name, age (~1851 birth from age 9), Pennsylvania birthplace, household position as child_1, shared Ackerman surname, consistency with George as father. For pe_005–pe_008 (Margaret): name, age (~1854 birth from age 6), Pennsylvania birthplace, household position as child_2, shared surname, consistency with George as father. All rationales address why competing candidates were ruled out (new stubs have no competing candidates; I1 is pre-existing and already linked). The rationales correctly note that I3 and I4 are new stubs minted from this persona, so match_score is null (circular). Relationship rationales (pe_004, pe_005, pe_009) explain that the 1860 census did not record relationships, so parentage is inferred from household position and shared surname—a key disambiguation step. Rationales are specific, not generic.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

No warnings on I1. Here is the full summary of what was done and what the evidence shows.

**Links created:**

| Assertion | Person | Confidence | Score | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| a_001–a_009 (Great Register 1875, registrant) | I1 Hermann Gaetjen | speculative | 0.43 | Namesake cap |
| a_010–a_014 (Germans to America Index, passenger) | I1 Hermann Gaetjen | speculative | 0.006 | Namesake cap + low score |

**Why both are speculative, not probable:**

The system enforces a namesake cap on I1 because two registered namesakes exist: one born in 1873 (who would have been only about one year old at the 1875 Great Register) and one born in 1827 (who would have been about 48 in 1875 and lived in Butte County). Although both namesakes are chronologically impossible for either record's person, the cap still applies mechanically until a tie exists — meaning a prior record already linked to I1 at `probable` or better that shares the same address or occupation, or another party of the same source linked to a spouse, parent, or child of I1. None of that tie exists yet, so both sources land at `speculative`.

**Why neither persona was put on a stub:**

The Great Register (score 0.43, moderate band, "matched: true") is the stronger result. The algorithm agrees on an identity match with I1. The only thing preventing `probable` is the namesake cap, not a qualitative conflict. A stub would fragment a record that is most likely about I1 and would need to be merged later anyway. Linking speculatively to I1 records the analytical finding and leaves the upgrade path clear.

The Germans to America Index (score 0.006, "matched: false") is genuinely weak algorithmically — the truncated name "Herm," the New York arrival rather than San Francisco data, and the thin index entry all suppress the score. The qualitative link to I1 runs through the Great Register: both records independently give birth year 1854 in a timeline consistent with I1 (NY 1871 → SF 1875 → first child 1878), and both namesakes are excluded by age. A stub for the immigration record would be misleading — the record is about the same person as the Great Register registrant — so the speculative link to I1 is the correct analytical record.

**Birth year discrepancy:**

Both records give birth year ~1854. I1's tree birth year is "about 1859" and is explicitly unsourced. The two records are more reliable than an unsourced estimate and almost certainly right. No core identifier conflict was declared because the tree estimate is the likely error, not the records.

**Facts not yet on the tree:**

Because all links are speculative, the Great Register and immigration facts (age ~21, fireman, 5 Cook Street SF, naturalized 13 Aug 1875 California 4th District Court; born ~1854 Prussia, arrived NY 2 Jun 1871) have not been materialized onto I1. They will be written once a tie lifts the links to `probable`.

**To lift the namesake cap:** Locate and link any record that independently ties the registrant to I1 specifically — for example, the underlying California 4th District Court naturalization record from 13 Aug 1875 (FamilySearch collection 2125028), which may name I1's wife Amelia or give a hometown, or an 1880 census entry showing Hermann Gaetjen in San Francisco with Amelia Nichols and Henry Joseph (born 1878). Either would supply the tie that raises the confidence.

---

Two records were connected, as best the available evidence allows, to Hermann Gaetjen — the 1875 San Francisco voter register entry for a 21-year-old fireman named Hermann Gatjen (a common spelling variant) living at 5 Cook Street, and a passenger index entry showing a "Herm Gaetjen" born in 1854 in Prussia arriving in New York in June 1871. Both records point to the same birth year of about 1854, and the timeline fits: New York in 1871, San Francisco by 1875, and children born there starting in 1878. The voter register was given a moderate similarity score by the identity-matching tool; the immigration index scored nearly zero, likely because it is a thin index entry with a truncated name and no San Francisco data. Because two other Hermann Gaetjens are recorded in California (one far too young, one far too old), the rules require both connections to be held at the lowest confidence level — "only possibly" — until a record surfaces that ties the voter register entry to Hermann's wife Amelia or one of his children, or that finds him in San Francisco with his family. The next step is to search for that naturalization record from the California 4th District Court dated 13 August 1875, or for the 1880 census household, which would provide that tie and let both records be upgraded to a stronger match.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

Search for a passenger list, naturalization record, or similar document placing the Weller family's emigration from England in the window between the 1861 English census and the 1870 American census. That will both confirm the family's identity and strengthen all 22 links.
